questions.knowledge_point: Understanding the Odd Extension of a Function
questions.problem: Let $F(x)=-2{x}^{3}+3x$ for $x\in [0,\pi ),$ and let $f(x)$ be the **odd** extension of $F(x)$ to $x\in (-\pi ,\pi ).$ What is $f(x)$ for $x\in (-\pi ,0)?$
questions.worked_solution:
If $F(x)$ is defined on $x\in [0,\pi ),$ the odd extension of $F$ is the function $f$ such that

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}F(x), & x\in [0,\pi ), \\ -F(-x), & x\in (-\pi ,0).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, for $x\in (-\pi ,0),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =-F(-x) \\  & =-(-2(-x)^{3}+3(-x)) \\  & =-(2{x}^{3}-3x) \\  & =-2{x}^{3}+3x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Sine Coefficients From the Half-Range Formula
questions.problem:
$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)
$$

Let $F(x)=-5x$ for $x\in [0,\pi ).$ The Fourier sine series of the **odd** $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is shown above. Find the expression for ${b}_{n}.$
$\,{b}_{n}=$ {{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
For our Fourier sine series, the coefficients are given by

$$
{b}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=-5x$ for $x\in (0,\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
{b}_{n}=-\frac{10}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }x\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\, & ⇒\,v=-\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{n} & =-\frac{10}{\pi }(uv\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =-\frac{10}{\pi }(-\frac{1}{n}[x\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{n}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{10}{n\pi }((\pi \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-0\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(0))-\frac{1}{n}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =\frac{10}{n\pi }(\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-\frac{1}{n}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))) \\  & =\frac{10\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )}{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )=(-1)^{n},$ we have

$$
{b}_{n}=\frac{10(-1)^{n}}{n}.
$$

questions.problem:
$$
f(x)∼{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{b}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)
$$

Let $F(x)=-2x+3$ for $x\in [0,\pi ).$ The Fourier sine series of the **odd** $2\pi $-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is shown above. Find the expression for ${b}_{n}.$$\,{b}_{n}=$ {{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
For our Fourier sine series, the coefficients are given by

$$
{b}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=-2x+3$ for $x\in (0,\pi ).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
{b}_{n}=\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(-2x+3)\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=-2x+3\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=-2 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\, & ⇒\,v=-\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{n} & =\frac{2}{\pi }(uv\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }(-\frac{1}{n}[(-2x+3)\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }-\frac{2}{n}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =-\frac{2}{n\pi }(((-2\pi +3)\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-3\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(0))+\frac{2}{n}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =-\frac{2}{n\pi }((-2\pi +3)\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-3+\frac{2}{n}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))) \\  & =-\frac{2}{n\pi }((-2\pi +3)\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-3).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )=(-1)^{n},$ we have

$$
{b}_{n}=-\frac{2}{n\pi }((-2\pi +3)(-1)^{n}-3)=\frac{2}{n\pi }((-1)^{n}(2\pi -3)+3).
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Let $F(x)=4x$ for $x\in[0,\pi).$ Find the missing parts in the Fourier sine series of the **odd** $2\pi$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of the function $F(x)$ below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14068497/assets/20ec903a94cb720f0d2c50b427409e36705af1f9f226b5c6fb11f93f92f0dd49.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
For our Fourier sine series, the coefficients are given by

$$
b_n=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\pi f(x)\sin(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=4x$ for $x \in (0,\pi).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get

$$
b_n = \dfrac{8}{\pi}\int_0^\pi x \sin(nx)\,\text{d}x.
$$

We use the integration by parts: 

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⇒\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)\, & ⇒\,v=-\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{b}_{n} & =\frac{8}{\pi }(uv\,{|}_{0}^{\pi }-{\int }_{0}^{\pi }v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\frac{8}{\pi }(-\frac{1}{n}[x\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }+\frac{1}{n}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(nx)\,\text{d}x) \\  & =-\frac{8}{n\pi }((\pi \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-0\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(0))-\frac{1}{n}[\operatorname{sin}⁡(nx)]_{0}^{\pi }) \\  & =-\frac{8}{n\pi }(\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )-\frac{1}{n}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(n\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))) \\  & =-\frac{8\operatorname{cos}⁡(n\pi )}{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, since $\cos(n\pi)=(-1)^n,$ we have

$$
b_n = -\dfrac{8(-1)^n}{n}=\dfrac{8(-1)^{n+1}}{n}.
$$

Finally, the Fourier sine series is

$$
f(x) \sim \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{8(-1)^{n+1}}{n} \cdot \sin(nx).
$$
